Issued at 135 AM MDT Sun Oct 25 2026

It was quite bright this evening when driving to work from my house 
to the humble Riverton weather abode to the west of town. This is 
courtesy of the almost full Hunters Moon, which peaks tomorrow night 
around midnight or so. Most areas would have a better chance of 
seeing it tonight though, as there will be a couple of systems 
impacting the area over the next couple of days.

The first system is an upper level low over Arizona that will lift 
northeast over the next couple of days. This system looks much more 
like a glancing blow as it will be weakening and the best forcing 
will remain to the south and east of the area. The best chance of 
showers will be from later this afternoon into tonight and 
especially from south of a Rock Springs to Casper line. This looks 
more like a minor nuisance system, All areas with the exception of 
the highest elevations of Casper Mountain and the Wind River Range 
have less than a 1 in 2 chance of a tenth of an inch of 
precipitation. Many locations will see nothing. The best chance of 
showers will be in southern Wyoming today, shifting toward Natrona 
as well as eastern portions of Fremont and Sweetwater Counties 
tonight. All showers should end by or shortly after sunrise Monday.
It will another cool day as well, with high temperatures similar to 
highs on Saturday.

The second, and more impactful system impacts the area from Monday 
night through Tuesday. This will be a fast moving low moving into 
the Pacific Northwest tonight and moving across the northern Rockies 
Monday night into Tuesday. This will set up the typical fall / 
winter westerly flow situation across the area, with most 
precipitation falling in western Wyoming with favorable orographics 
and wind being the main impact East of the Divide. With this being 
the heart of football season, we will tackle each of these threats 
individually, but hopefully not be penalized for being wrong.

We will start with the precipitation, which includes some 
accumulating snow, maybe even for the lower elevations. Most of the 
western mountains have a nearly 100 percent chance of a tenth of an 
inch of QPF or more from Monday night through Tuesday. The area with 
a greater than 1 in 2 chance of a third of an inch of QPF or greater 
is where you would expect it with a west to southwest flow, mainly 
from the northern Salt and Wyoming Range through the Tetons and 
southwestern Yellowstone Park. Amounts have increased somewhat from 
yesterday, with a decent amount of the aforementioned area having a 
greater than 1 in 2 chance of a half an inch or more. There will be 
some decent upper level forcing with this system, with an 100 to 110 
knot jet streak moving over the area, enhancing precipitation rates. 
The limiting factor will be the speed of the system, with most of 
the precipitation falling in a period from later Sunday evening 
through sunrise on Monday. 

But the main question everyone is wondering about it the potential 
for snow. One factor will be how fast a cold front can move through 
and lower snow levels. Through most of Monday evening, 700 millibar 
temperatures would likely remain at 0 celsius or higher, keeping 
snow levels at 8500 feet or higher. The main time of snow 
accumulation would be from midnight Sunday night through sunrise 
Monday, when 700 millibar temperatures fall as low as minus 5 to 
minus 6, which would lower snow levels to valley floors. Most 
locations, including portions of the Jackson and Star Valleys have 
at least a 1 in 2 chance of an inch of snow or more. As for the 
chance of 3 inches, the 1 in 2 probability is generally around 7500 
feet or higher, which includes places like Teton and Togwotee 
Passes. The mountain advisory amount is 6 inches, and the chance of 
this is mainly above 10000 feet where impacts are minimal. However, 
with the jet overhead, there will be a fair amount of wind that 
could bring some blowing snow. As for potential highlights, the 
chance is around 2 out of 5 for advisories, probably from Sunday 
night into midday Monday. We won't issue any yet but future shifts 
will have to take a closer look. Most lower elevation areas would 
have few impacts, but there could be a small accumulation of snow in 
places like Big Piney, Pinedale or Dubois later Monday night or 
Tuesday morning.

In areas East of the Divide, the main concerns shifts to strong to 
potential high wind. The pressure gradient will tighten ahead of the 
cold front. And, with a combination of the jet overhead and 700 
millibar winds climbing as high as 55 knots, things will get quite 
blustery. A large portion of areas East of the Divide have at least 
a 1 in 2 chance of wind gusts over 40 mph. The core of the highest 
wind is where you would expect it in this pattern, from Muddy Gap 
through Casper, where there is a greater than 1 in 2 chance of wind 
gusts past 55 mph. The current forecast has borderline high wind,
